subject: Follow-up: connection occupancy & parallel request sizing for BrightView POC
messages:
From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com>
To: Amanda Chen <amanda.chen@brightviewhealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 May 2029 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Follow-up: connection occupancy & parallel request sizing for BrightView POC

Hi Amanda —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and the asks we promised to surface internally. Short version first: we think the POC can meet BrightView's 99th %-tile latency target (<= 120ms for short completion calls) with the right connection multiplexing and a 250-concurrency reservation for the steady-state workload; burst headroom of 1.5x for traffic spikes.

Notes from the call:
- BrightView expected steady QPS: 420 QPS during business hours (US-east).
- Typical request profile: 60% short-completions (<= 64 tokens), 30% streaming sessions (chat with partial token streaming), 10% long generation (>= 512 tokens).
- SLOs: 99th %-tile latency <= 120ms for short calls; streaming first-byte <= 200ms; sustained throughput target 15k tokens/s.
- Current integration: server-side SDK with persistent websockets; you prefer connection pooling over opening ephemeral sockets per request.

Open asks to confirm for Redwood ops:
1) Can BrightView accept a warm-connection pool model (shared connections with multiplexing, client maintains session affinity)?
2) Do you control per-session concurrency (client-side queue) or do you want Redwood to enforce per-API-key throttles?
3) Any regulatory requirement around connection logging/visibility (we can enable additional audit headers if needed)?

Next steps from our side: we will provide a suggested connection occupancy matrix and a small sample CSV with expected socket counts under different pooling strategies (attached). Also including a short note on how our rate-limit tiers map to the occupancy model.

Attached: redwood-conn-profile-brief.pdf, bv-conn-occupancy-sample.csv

Can you confirm the steady QPS and whether you expect any nightly batch spikes? If acceptable, we propose locking an initial dedicated pool of 250 concurrent sessions for the POC and enabling a 1.5x burst for 10-minute windows.

Thanks —
Soojin

--
Soojin Lee

From: Amanda Chen <amanda.chen@brightviewhealth.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com>
Cc: Platform Ops <platform-ops@brightviewhealth.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 May 2029 11:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: connection occupancy & parallel request sizing for BrightView POC

Thanks, Soojin — this is very helpful. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Steady QPS is accurate — 420 QPS during 8am-6pm ET (we operate central US with traffic skew). Expect an additional nightly batch at ~02:00 ET that could double short bursts for ~20 minutes (we'll send exact cron info).
- For streaming calls, user agents open a web socket and we stream tokens as they are generated. We want to preserve per-user session ordering (so session affinity is required).
- We prefer Redwood to enforce token-level throttles on your side rather than building a custom queue; easier for our ops.

One security note: our compliance team needs audit logs that show connection ID and request UUID for 30 days for the POC. Will that be available from the private control plane?

A couple of asks back to Redwood:
1) Please provide the expected socket pool size under the warm-connection (mux) model for both steady-state and burst.
2) Confirm how rate limits (requests/sec and concurrent sessions) translate to per-connection multiplexing limits.
3) Any impact on streaming first-byte latency when multiplexing?

We'll loop in Jake (platform-ops) for the audit log requirement.

—Amanda

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com>
To: Amanda Chen <amanda.chen@brightviewhealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 May 2029 13:48:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: connection occupancy & parallel request sizing for BrightView POC

Amanda —

Appreciate the clarifications. Short answers up front: yes to session affinity support, yes we can surface connection ID + request UUID in audit logs for 30 days on the private control plane, and multiplexing should not materially impact first-byte latency for streaming if we reserve enough sockets and prioritize first-byte traffic.

Sizing guidance (see attached CSV for worked examples):
- Warm-connection multiplexing model: target 40 concurrent logical streams per socket for mixed workloads.
- Steady state: 420 QPS with 40 streams/socket => ~11 sockets sustained. We add headroom for session affinity and burst fragmentation (sessions pinned to sockets) so recommended reserved sockets = 60 for POC.
- Burst (2x QPS for 20 minutes) => ~120 sockets recommended to keep 99th %-tile latency within target.
- Concurrency reservation proposal: 250 logical concurrent request allowance (this is the control-plane reservation; maps to ~7-8x the reserved sockets depending on multiplexing). We'll document the exact mapping in the rate-card snippet.

Important notes on rate-limits:
- Redwood enforces two axes: token throughput (tokens/s per model endpoint) and session concurrency (logical concurrent request slots).
- For streaming workloads, we prioritize first-byte/TTFB by giving small bursts of compute to initial tokens which helps keep first-byte under 200ms; continuous long generations are metered on tokens/s.

Proposed action items:
1) Redwood will provision a temporary POC pool: 60 reserved sockets, 250 logical concurrency, burst headroom enabled to 1.5x for 15-minute windows.
2) We'll enable audit logging (connection ID + request UUID) for 30 days and share the export instructions with Jake.
3) Marissa will prepare a short test plan (load profile + success criteria) and we'll run a 2-hour soak that includes the nightly batch spike emulation.

If that sounds reasonable we can push a provisioning request this afternoon.

Soojin

--
Soojin Lee
Enterprise Solutions | Redwood Inference

From: Jake Torres <jake.torres@brightviewhealth.com>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 15 May 2029 15:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: connection occupancy & parallel request sizing for BrightView POC

Hey team — thanks for the clear plan. A couple quick notes from Platform Ops: 

- Audit logs: 30-day retention is fine. We will want a daily S3 export for the POC (log format with connection_id, request_uuid, timestamp, user_id). Can you confirm Redwood's export format?
- For connection counts: the numbers you proposed look reasonable; we may start with 80 reserved sockets to keep session affinity strict and then drop to 60 after the first week if everything is stable.
- On throttling: we'd like Redwood to enforce a soft backpressure at 230 logical concurrency and a hard rejection at 270, so we can surface 429 states to the client and perform graceful degradation. Is that enforceable?

If Redwood can support S3 daily export and the backpressure thresholds above, we are good to kick off the POC. I'll prepare a short runbook for the soak tomorrow.

—Jake
Platform Ops — BrightView Health
platform-ops@brightviewhealth.com

On Wed, May 15, 2029 at 10:12 AM Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com> wrote:
> Thanks Jake — we can do both items.
> 
> - Export format: newline-delimited JSON (ndjson) with fields: connection_id, request_uuid, ts, model, endpoint, tokens_in, tokens_out. We'll provide the S3 bucket policy template for the export.
> - Backpressure: yes — we can configure a soft threshold at 230 logical concurrency (signals 429 with Retry-After header) and a hard 270 (reject). We'll implement Grafana alerts and a webhook to your ops when thresholds cross 85%.
> 
> I'll open the provisioning ticket now.
> 
> Soojin
